analysis.one_liner: Imposes a 100 percent excise tax on windfall profits from wholesale electricity sold in the West.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee and died there without ever receiving a committee or floor vote before the 106th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: During a period when wholesale electricity prices in the western United States spiked, this bill would have placed a 100 percent tax on any profit sellers made above either the cost-based rate set under the Federal Power Act or the region's average wholesale price from the three years before June 2000, whichever was lower. The sellers, not buyers, would owe the tax. It was introduced by Rep. Bob Filner with Rep. Dennis Kucinich in October 2000 and never moved past the committee it was assigned to.
analysis.who_benefits: Electricity consumers in the western states, who would benefit from a tax that removes the profit on prices above cost-based or historical levels, and federal taxpayers, who would receive the revenue from the excise tax.

how_it_helps.text: The bill imposes an excise tax equal to 100 percent of the windfall profit from wholesale electricity sales in the Western System Coordinating Council, defined as profits above the lesser of a cost-based rate under the Federal Power Act or the region's average wholesale price over the three years before June 1, 2000.
The tax is paid by the seller, so it directly claws back excess profits from wholesale electricity sellers rather than raising costs for buyers.
It applies to electricity sold after June 1, 2000, reaching the price spikes that had already occurred in the region that year.

analysis.who_pays: Wholesale electricity sellers and energy trading firms operating in the western grid, which would surrender every dollar of profit above the cost-based or historical price benchmark.

drawbacks.text: A 100 percent tax on any price above a benchmark gives sellers no reward for selling at more than the reference price, which could discourage new electricity supply precisely when shortages are driving prices up; an honest supporter would acknowledge that risk.
The tax applies retroactively to electricity sold after June 1, 2000, and companies selling during that period would owe taxes on transactions already completed, raising fairness and legal questions.
The bill addresses only wholesale sales in the Western System Coordinating Council, so it does nothing about retail rates or about price spikes elsewhere.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For consumers in the western states facing sharply higher wholesale power prices, the tax would have returned windfall profits to the Treasury and removed the payoff for extreme pricing. The design is crude: taxing all profit above a benchmark at 100 percent could deter investment in generation during a shortage, and the retroactive reach to mid-2000 would tax completed sales. On balance the bill's aim was to protect ratepayers from price spikes, but its blunt mechanism carried real supply-side risk.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Ways and Means Committee on October 6, 2000, and the committee never acted on it before the 106th Congress expired in January 2001.

narrative.text: Rep. Bob Filner introduced the bill on October 6, 2000, for himself and Rep. Dennis Kucinich.
The bill would have imposed a 100 percent excise tax on windfall profits from wholesale electricity sales in the Western System Coordinating Council.
The House referred it to the Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced, and the action history shows no further action of any kind.
The 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001, so the bill died in committee without a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Wholesale electricity sellers in the West kept their windfall profits from the 2000 price spikes, because the Ways and Means Committee never acted and the bill died with the Congress.

for.name: Rep. Bob Filner
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on October 6, 2000, to tax windfall profits from western wholesale electricity sales.

for.name: Rep. Dennis Kucinich
for.role: Original cosponsor, U.S. House of Representatives (OH)
for.what_they_did: Joined as the bill's sole cosponsor when it was introduced.

against.name: Bill Archer
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a committee markup; it sat in committee until the Congress ended.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction for tax legislation
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on October 6, 2000, and took no action on it before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: Only two Democrats are on record supporting the bill and no Republican is recorded as taking any position; the bill died in a Republican-chaired committee without any vote that would show the split.

industries.industry: Wholesale electricity sellers and energy traders in the western grid
industries.note: The bill would have taxed away 100 percent of their profits above cost-based or historical price benchmarks for sales after June 1, 2000, directly targeting sellers who benefited from the western price spikes. Ordinary consumers paid those elevated prices, so the industry's interest in blocking the bill ran against ratepayers.

industries.industry: Electric utilities and power marketers investing in new western generation
industries.note: Any seller would have faced the tax, and the prospect of keeping none of the profit above the benchmark could reduce the incentive to build or sell extra power during shortages, which would hurt the same consumers the tax was meant to protect.
